ana-g16-c22.why: The posterior temporalis fibres run nearly horizontally towards the mandibular coronoid process, so their contraction pulls the mandible backwards; the anterior fibres mainly elevate it.

notes.A: Bilateral contraction of the lateral pterygoids pulls the condyles forwards, which protrudes the jaw and assists opening.
notes.B: Masseter principally elevates the mandible to close the jaw, although its deep fibres can assist retraction.
notes.C: Mylohyoid elevates the floor of the mouth and hyoid during swallowing rather than retracting the mandible.
notes.D: Medial pterygoid elevates and assists protrusion of the mandible rather than being its principal retractor.

ana-g16-c24.why: Zygomaticus major is a muscle of facial expression that draws the angle of the mouth upwards and laterally. Buccinator, despite its facial nerve supply, assists chewing by keeping food between the teeth.

notes.B: Temporalis elevates the mandible during chewing, and its posterior fibres also retract the jaw.
notes.C: Lateral pterygoid protrudes the mandible and produces side-to-side grinding movements during mastication.
notes.D: Medial pterygoid elevates the mandible and assists protrusion and side-to-side grinding during chewing.
notes.E: Buccinator presses the cheek against the teeth, returning food to the occlusal surfaces during chewing.

ana-g16-c32.why: The deep head of medial pterygoid arises from the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate and inserts on the medial mandibular ramus, giving it a strong jaw-elevating action.

notes.A: The posterior temporalis fibres pull the coronoid process backwards and are the principal mandibular retractors.
notes.B: Levator veli palatini elevates the soft palate during swallowing and does not move the mandible.
notes.C: Lateral pterygoid principally protrudes the mandible and arises partly from the lateral surface of the lateral pterygoid plate.
notes.D: Tensor veli palatini tenses the palatal aponeurosis by pulling its tendon around the pterygoid hamulus.

ana-g16-p34.why: Piriformis lines the posterior pelvic wall and laterally rotates the hip. The pelvic diaphragm instead comprises levator ani, including its three subdivisions, and coccygeus.

notes.A: Pubococcygeus is a medial component of levator ani that supports the pelvic viscera and contributes to the pelvic floor.
notes.B: Coccygeus extends from the ischial spine towards the sacrum and coccyx, completing the posterior pelvic diaphragm.
notes.D: Puborectalis is the U-shaped part of levator ani that maintains the anorectal angle and helps support continence.
notes.E: Iliococcygeus forms the thinner lateral portion of levator ani and contributes to the supporting pelvic diaphragm.

ana-g16-p35.why: Obturator internus arises from the inner surface of the obturator membrane and surrounding bones, forming the muscular lateral pelvic wall. Its fascia provides attachment for levator ani.

notes.B: Piriformis is a muscle on the anterior surface of the sacrum, forming part of the posterior rather than lateral pelvic wall.
notes.C: Pubococcygeus forms part of levator ani and supports the pelvic viscera from below rather than lining the side wall.
notes.D: Iliococcygeus arises from the tendinous arch of obturator fascia but belongs to the pelvic diaphragm, not the lateral wall.
notes.E: Ischiococcygeus, also called coccygeus, completes the posterior pelvic floor rather than covering the lateral wall.

ana-g16-p50.why: Ischiocavernosus covers the crus of the penis or clitoris along the ischiopubic ramus, rather than joining the central fibromuscular perineal body where several other perineal muscles converge.

notes.B: Bulbospongiosus attaches to the perineal body posteriorly, linking the superficial perineal musculature to this central support.
notes.C: The superficial transverse perineal muscle runs medially towards the perineal body, where its fibres help stabilise the central attachment.
notes.D: The deep transverse perineal muscle contributes fibres to the perineal body and helps support the pelvic outlet.
notes.E: The anterior fibres of the external anal sphincter attach to the perineal body, linking it to the continence mechanism.

ana-g16-k83.why: The anatomical snuffbox lies between the tendon of extensor pollicis longus medially and the paired tendons of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis laterally.

notes.A: Extensor pollicis longus turns around the dorsal radial tubercle to form the medial boundary of the snuffbox.
notes.B: Abductor pollicis longus travels with extensor pollicis brevis along the lateral boundary of the anatomical snuffbox.
notes.C: Extensor pollicis brevis accompanies abductor pollicis longus and forms the radial, not ulnar, boundary of the snuffbox.

ana-g16-k99.why: The inferior rectal nerve is a branch of the pudendal nerve that supplies the external anal sphincter and carries sensation from the perianal skin and lower anal canal.

notes.A: Levator ani receives its principal motor supply from direct sacral branches, chiefly S3 and S4, rather than the inferior rectal nerve.
notes.B: The inferior rectal nerve supplies the voluntary external anal sphincter, so injury weakens voluntary closure of the anal canal.
notes.C: The perineal body is a fibromuscular attachment point rather than an independently innervated skeletal muscle.

ana-g16-t29.why: Ribs divide the thoracic wall into intercostal spaces, and its innermost muscular layer has three regional components. Both thoracic and abdominal walls share segmental innervation and a neurovascular plane between their middle and deepest muscle layers.

notes.A: The ribs interrupt the thoracic muscle sheets, producing separate intercostal muscles in each intercostal space.
notes.B: Both walls are segmentally supplied, so this is not a difference; the abdominal wall receives thoracoabdominal nerves and upper lumbar branches.
notes.C: The innermost thoracic layer consists of innermost intercostals laterally, subcostales posteriorly and transversus thoracis anteriorly.
notes.D: The main neurovascular plane lies between internal and innermost intercostals in the thorax, and internal oblique and transversus abdominis in the abdomen.
notes.E: The thoracic external intercostals occupy multiple separate spaces, whereas external oblique forms a broad continuous abdominal muscle sheet.

ana-g16-t30.why: The intercostal muscular layers support rib movements and protect the neurovascular bundle. Each typical intercostal nerve carries motor and sensory fibres and ends anteriorly as a cutaneous branch.

notes.A: External intercostal muscle fibres terminate anteriorly near the costochondral junction and continue towards the sternum as the external intercostal membrane.
notes.B: The deepest thoracic muscle layer is divided regionally into innermost intercostals, subcostales and transversus thoracis.
notes.C: Intercostal nerves carry motor fibres to the thoracic muscles and sensory fibres from skin and parietal pleura.
notes.D: The innermost intercostals occupy the lateral parts of the intercostal spaces, deep to the main neurovascular bundle.
notes.E: A typical intercostal nerve ends as an anterior cutaneous branch supplying skin near the sternum, after giving muscular branches.

ana-ms15-t21.why: The femoral triangle is a subinguinal region through which the femoral neurovascular structures enter the thigh. Its apex continues into the adductor canal and its fascia contains the saphenous opening.

notes.A: The inguinal ligament extends between the anterior superior iliac spine and pubic tubercle, forming the superior boundary of the triangle.
notes.B: The medial edge of sartorius forms the lateral boundary and converges with adductor longus at the apex.
notes.C: Pectineus contributes to the medial floor, while iliacus and psoas major form the floor further laterally.
notes.D: The apex leads into the adductor canal, which carries the femoral vessels deeper into the thigh.
notes.E: The great saphenous vein passes through the saphenous opening in the fascia lata to join the femoral vein within the triangle.

ana-ms15-t126.why: Hernias can occur where the abdominal wall or diaphragm has natural openings or weak regions. These defects permit tissue or viscera to protrude beyond their usual anatomical compartment.

notes.A: An umbilical hernia protrudes through a weakness in the umbilical ring or adjacent abdominal wall.
notes.B: Lumbar hernias protrude through weak regions of the posterolateral abdominal wall, including the lumbar triangles.
notes.C: An obturator hernia passes through the obturator canal alongside the obturator nerve and vessels, within the obturator foramen.
notes.D: A femoral hernia enters the femoral ring and canal, medial to the femoral vein and below the inguinal ligament.
notes.E: A hiatus hernia occurs when part of the stomach passes through the oesophageal hiatus into the thoracic cavity.

ana-ms15-t131.why: The inguinal triangle lies medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, lateral to rectus abdominis and above the inguinal ligament. Its transversalis fascia is a potential weakness through which direct inguinal hernias protrude.

notes.A: The inferior epigastric vessels ascend superomedially and form the lateral boundary of the inguinal triangle.
notes.B: The lateral border of rectus abdominis forms the medial boundary of the triangle near the midline.
notes.C: The medial portion of the inguinal ligament forms the inferior boundary of the triangle, close to the pubic tubercle.
notes.D: The ligament forms the inferior base and the inferior epigastric vessels converge towards the rectus border superiorly, producing an upward apex.
notes.E: Arched fibres of internal oblique contribute to the roof of the inguinal canal, superficial to the transversalis fascia of the triangle.

ana-gpq-32.why: Erector spinae has three columns: iliocostalis (lateral), longissimus (middle) and spinalis (medial); semispinalis, multifidus and rotatores are the deeper transversospinalis group.

notes.A: Longissimus occupies the intermediate column and spans more of the back than the medial spinalis column.
notes.B: Spinalis is the medial column closest to the spinous processes and helps extend the vertebral column.
notes.C: Semispinalis belongs to the deeper transversospinalis group and its fibres course towards spinous processes several levels above.
notes.D: Multifidus belongs to the transversospinalis group and stabilises vertebral segments through its short, obliquely directed fascicles.
notes.E: Rotatores are the deepest transversospinalis muscles, connecting transverse processes to vertebral laminae at nearby levels.

ana-gpq-34.why: The suboccipital triangle contains the vertebral artery and suboccipital nerve. Three short muscles bound it, while the atlas and posterior atlanto-occipital membrane form its floor.

notes.A: Rectus capitis posterior major forms the superomedial border; obliquus capitis superior forms the superolateral border.
notes.B: Obliquus capitis superior forms the superolateral border rather than rectus capitis posterior major, which lies medially.
notes.C: Obliquus capitis inferior extends between the axis and atlas to form the inferior boundary of the triangle.
notes.D: The posterior atlanto-occipital membrane and posterior arch of the atlas underlie the muscular boundaries of the triangle.
notes.E: The traditional midline cisternal puncture targets the cisterna magna. The paired muscular triangles lie lateral to that midline landmark.

ana-gpq-38.why: Skeletal muscle fibres may be classified by contractile and metabolic properties or by whether they lie inside or outside muscle spindles. Collagen fibres and whole sensory receptors are different structures.

notes.A: Sharpey’s fibres are collagen bundles that anchor periosteum, tendons or ligaments to bone, rather than contractile muscle fibres.
notes.B: Slow type I fibres rely strongly on oxidative metabolism and resist fatigue during sustained low-force contraction.
notes.C: Intrafusal muscle fibres lie within muscle spindles and help the receptor detect changes in skeletal muscle length.
notes.D: Extrafusal muscle fibres lie outside spindles and generate the force responsible for skeletal muscle movement.
notes.E: A muscle spindle is a sensory receptor organ containing intrafusal fibres and sensory nerve endings, not an individual muscle fibre.

ana-gpq-39.why: Muscle contraction can be classified by changes in muscle length and tension, or by the pattern of activation over time. These classifications describe different aspects of muscular activity.

notes.A: An eccentric contraction develops active tension while the muscle lengthens, as when controlling the descent of a load.
notes.B: A concentric contraction produces active shortening when muscle force overcomes the opposing load.
notes.C: An isometric contraction develops or maintains tension without an appreciable change in overall muscle length.
notes.D: A phasic contraction is a relatively brief episode of activity, contrasted with sustained tonic contraction.
notes.E: An isotonic contraction involves a change in muscle length at approximately constant tension under idealised conditions.

ana-gpq-40.why: A fist requires flexion of the fingers and thumb. The long digital flexors cross the relevant joints to bend the digits, while forearm pronators and wrist flexors act at different joints.

notes.A: Flexor digitorum profundus flexes the distal interphalangeal joints of the fingers and assists flexion at more proximal joints.
notes.B: Pronator teres rotates the forearm into pronation and does not directly flex the fingers into a fist.
notes.C: Flexor carpi radialis flexes and abducts the wrist, but it has no insertion on the digital phalanges.
notes.D: Flexor pollicis longus bends the thumb at its interphalangeal joint, contributing to thumb flexion during gripping.
notes.E: Flexor digitorum superficialis flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints of the four fingers during formation of a fist.

ana-gpq-41.why: Wrist extension places the long finger flexors at a more favourable length for forceful gripping. Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis stabilise the wrist while the fingers flex.

notes.A: Flexor digitorum superficialis is a prime mover of finger flexion rather than a wrist-extending stabiliser during gripping.
notes.B: Flexor carpi ulnaris flexes and adducts the wrist, opposing the extension required to optimise the finger flexors’ length.
notes.C: Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis extend and stabilise the wrist, improving the length–tension relationship of the digital flexors.
notes.D: Extensor digiti minimi chiefly extends the little finger rather than acting as a principal wrist stabiliser for gripping.
notes.E: Extensor indicis chiefly extends the index finger independently rather than holding the wrist extended during a strong grip.

ana-gpq-45.why: The diaphragm has sternal, costal and lumbar muscular origins that converge on a common central tendon. This arrangement allows contraction to flatten the domes and increase thoracic volume.

notes.A: The sternal part arises from the posterior aspect of the xiphoid process and passes towards the central tendon.
notes.B: The costal part arises from the inner surfaces of the lower six ribs and their costal cartilages.
notes.C: The lumbar part arises from the lumbar vertebrae through the crura and from the arcuate ligaments.

ana-gpq-47.why: The three major diaphragmatic openings occur at characteristic levels: the caval opening at T8, the oesophageal hiatus at T10 and the aortic hiatus at T12.

notes.A: The aorta enters the abdomen at approximately T12, between the crura and beneath the median arcuate ligament.
notes.B: The aortic hiatus lies at T12 between the diaphragmatic crura beneath the median arcuate ligament.
notes.C: The oesophageal hiatus lies at T10 within the muscular diaphragm; T8 corresponds to the caval opening.
notes.D: The caval opening lies at T8 in the central tendon; T10 corresponds to the oesophageal hiatus.
notes.E: The sternocostal gap lies between the sternal and costal origins of the diaphragm, near the xiphoid rather than at a standard vertebral level.

ana-gpq-48.why: The aortic hiatus is posterior to the diaphragm beneath the median arcuate ligament and transmits the aorta and thoracic duct. The azygos vein may accompany them or pass separately.

notes.A: The sympathetic trunks pass posterior to the medial arcuate ligaments rather than through the central aortic hiatus.
notes.B: The azygos vein may enter the thorax through the aortic hiatus, although it can also pierce the right crus.
notes.C: The thoracic duct ascends from the cisterna chyli through the aortic hiatus alongside the aorta.
notes.D: The greater splanchnic nerve usually pierces the diaphragmatic crus on its way to prevertebral ganglia.
notes.E: The abdominal aorta continues from the thoracic aorta through the hiatus beneath the median arcuate ligament at T12.

ana-gpq-49.why: The caval opening at T8 is within the central tendon and transmits the inferior vena cava, branches of the right phrenic nerve and associated hepatic lymphatics.

notes.A: The superior vena cava drains blood from the upper body directly into the right atrium without passing through the diaphragm.
notes.B: Branches of the right phrenic nerve accompany the inferior vena cava through the central tendon to supply the diaphragm.
notes.C: The inferior phrenic arteries generally arise within the abdomen and supply the inferior surface of the diaphragm.
notes.D: The right vagus contributes to the posterior vagal trunk, which enters the abdomen through the oesophageal hiatus.
notes.E: Some hepatic lymphatics accompany the inferior vena cava through the caval opening towards mediastinal lymphatic channels.

ana-gpq-50.why: The oesophageal hiatus is a muscular opening at T10 that transmits the oesophagus, anterior and posterior vagal trunks, and small vessels supplying the abdominal oesophagus.

notes.A: The anterior and posterior vagal trunks descend along the oesophagus and enter the abdomen through its diaphragmatic hiatus.
notes.B: The oesophagus traverses the muscular hiatus before joining the stomach at the gastro-oesophageal junction.
notes.C: The left phrenic nerve usually pierces the muscular diaphragm independently rather than following the oesophagus through its hiatus.
notes.D: The superior epigastric vessels pass through the sternocostal region to reach the anterior abdominal wall rather than the oesophageal hiatus.
notes.E: Small oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels accompany the abdominal oesophagus through the diaphragmatic hiatus.

ana-gpq-51.why: The resting position of the diaphragm reflects a balance between thoracic and abdominal forces and its own muscle tone. Loss of phrenic motor supply can elevate the affected hemidiaphragm.

notes.A: Abdominal muscle tone increases intra-abdominal pressure and can push the relaxed diaphragm upwards into the thorax.
notes.B: Elastic recoil of the lungs contributes to the pressure and mechanical forces acting on the diaphragm.
notes.C: Negative intrathoracic pressure contributes to the pressure gradient across the diaphragm and influences its resting position.
notes.D: Abdominal viscera exert upward pressure on the diaphragmatic domes, particularly when intra-abdominal pressure is increased.
notes.E: Unilateral phrenic paralysis removes active contraction from one hemidiaphragm, which may become elevated and move paradoxically during inspiration.

ana-gpq-52.why: Inspiration enlarges the thoracic cavity through diaphragmatic descent and rib elevation. During forced expiration, the interosseous internal intercostals help depress the ribs, while the relaxed diaphragm moves upwards.

notes.A: External intercostals assist inspiration by elevating the ribs and increasing the dimensions of the thoracic cavity.
notes.B: The interosseous portions of internal intercostals help depress the ribs during active or forced expiration.
notes.C: The interosseous internal intercostals generally assist forced expiration. The interchondral portion can aid inspiration, so the effect depends on the portion.
notes.D: Contraction flattens the diaphragmatic domes and increases, rather than reduces, the vertical dimension of the thoracic cavity.
notes.E: The transverse thoracic diameter increases through active rib elevation, particularly the bucket-handle movements of lower ribs.

ana-gpq-53.why: Accessory respiratory muscles supplement the primary respiratory muscles when ventilation or pressure generation must increase. Some elevate the rib cage during inspiration, while abdominal muscles assist forceful expiration and straining.

notes.A: Heavy exercise raises ventilatory demand, recruiting muscles such as sternocleidomastoid and the scalenes to assist inspiration.
notes.B: Airway obstruction increases the work of breathing, so accessory respiratory muscles may be recruited to generate greater pressure changes.
notes.C: During heavy lifting, respiratory and trunk muscles can stabilise the thorax and increase intra-abdominal pressure.
notes.D: Breathlessness in cardiac failure may increase the work of breathing and lead to recruitment of accessory inspiratory muscles.
notes.E: During labour, abdominal muscle contraction contributes to expulsive efforts by raising intra-abdominal pressure against a stabilised thorax.

ana-gpq-54.why: Accessory inspiratory muscles help expand the thoracic cage when ventilatory demand increases. They elevate or stabilise the ribs and sternum, whereas the abdominal muscles principally assist forced expiration.

notes.A: Sternocleidomastoid elevates the sternum and medial clavicle when its cranial attachment is fixed, assisting deep inspiration.
notes.B: The scalenes elevate or stabilise the first two ribs, helping expand the thoracic cage during inspiration.
notes.C: With the scapula fixed, serratus anterior can pull on the ribs and contribute to laboured inspiration.
notes.D: Rhomboids chiefly move and stabilise the scapula. They are outside the usual list of muscles that elevate the ribs in laboured inspiration.
notes.E: Abdominal muscles increase abdominal pressure and push the relaxed diaphragm upwards, helping force air out during active expiration.

ana-gpq-55.why: Extrinsic muscles of the back connect the axial skeleton to the scapula or humerus. They transmit force from the vertebral column to the upper limb, whereas pectoralis major principally connects the anterior thorax to the humerus.

notes.A: Rhomboid major extends from thoracic spinous processes to the medial scapular border, linking the scapula to the vertebral column.
notes.B: Latissimus dorsi arises partly from the lower vertebral region through the thoracolumbar fascia and inserts on the humerus.
notes.C: Pectoralis major originates from the clavicle, sternum and anterior costal region rather than directly from the vertebral column.
notes.D: Levator scapulae extends from upper cervical transverse processes to the superior medial border of the scapula.
notes.E: Trapezius attaches to the cervical and thoracic midline and inserts on the clavicle, acromion and scapular spine.

ana-gpq-56.why: The triangle of auscultation is a relatively thin muscular window on the posterior thorax, bounded by trapezius, latissimus dorsi and the scapula. Moving the scapula laterally improves access to breath sounds.

notes.A: Muscle coverage is relatively thin in the triangle, permitting easier transmission of breath sounds to the chest surface.
notes.B: The lateral edge of the lower trapezius forms the superomedial boundary of the triangle.
notes.C: Latissimus dorsi forms the inferior boundary, whereas rhomboid major contributes to the muscular floor.
notes.D: The triangle commonly overlies the sixth intercostal region, allowing auscultation through a relatively thin part of the posterior chest wall.
notes.E: The medial border of the scapula forms the lateral boundary and moves laterally when the shoulders are protracted.

ana-gpq-57.why: The rotator cuff consists of supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis. Their tendons blend with the glenohumeral capsule and dynamically stabilise the humeral head during shoulder movement.

notes.A: Teres major adducts and medially rotates the humerus, but its tendon does not contribute to the rotator cuff.
notes.B: Pectoralis minor attaches to the coracoid process and moves the scapula rather than reinforcing the glenohumeral capsule.
notes.C: Supraspinatus inserts on the superior facet of the greater tubercle and assists initiation of abduction while stabilising the humeral head.
notes.D: Subscapularis inserts on the lesser tubercle and reinforces the anterior shoulder capsule while medially rotating the humerus.
notes.E: Teres minor inserts on the inferior facet of the greater tubercle and reinforces the posterior shoulder capsule while laterally rotating the humerus.

ana-gpq-58.why: The clavipectoral fascia lies deep to pectoralis major and encloses subclavius and pectoralis minor. Its inferior extension supports the axillary floor, and several vessels and nerves pierce it.

notes.A: The costocoracoid portion of the fascia spans the region below the clavicle towards the coracoid process.
notes.B: The fascia splits around subclavius beneath the clavicle and reunites below the muscle.
notes.C: Pectoralis major has its own investing fascia; the clavipectoral fascia lies deep to it and encloses pectoralis minor instead.
notes.D: The inferior extension of clavipectoral fascia attaches to the axillary fascia and supports the axillary floor as its suspensory ligament.
notes.E: The cephalic vein pierces the clavipectoral fascia to join the axillary vein, whereas the basilic vein joins the brachial veins more distally.

ana-gpq-59.why: The scapular spaces transmit distinct neurovascular bundles between the shoulder and adjacent regions. Their contents can be distinguished by the muscular and bony boundaries through which each bundle travels.

notes.A: The suprascapular nerve passes beneath the superior transverse scapular ligament through the notch, while the artery usually passes above it.
notes.B: The axillary nerve travels through the quadrangular space with the posterior circumflex humeral vessels to reach the deltoid region.
notes.C: The circumflex scapular artery traverses the medial triangular space to reach the posterior scapular surface and join the scapular anastomosis.
notes.D: The profunda brachii artery accompanies the radial nerve through the triangular interval towards the posterior arm.
notes.E: The posterior circumflex humeral artery accompanies the axillary nerve through the quadrangular space; the anterior vessel passes anteriorly around the humerus.

ana-gpq-60.why: The quadrangular space is a passage bounded by teres minor, teres major, the long head of triceps and the surgical neck of the humerus. It transmits the axillary neurovascular bundle.

notes.A: The surgical neck of the humerus forms the lateral bony boundary of the quadrangular space.
notes.B: Viewed posteriorly, teres minor forms the superior muscular boundary of the quadrangular space.
notes.C: The long head of triceps separates the quadrangular space laterally from the medial triangular space.
notes.D: Teres major forms the inferior boundary of the quadrangular space and separates it from the triangular interval below.
notes.E: The radial nerve passes through the triangular interval with the profunda brachii artery, not the quadrangular space.

ana-gpq-61.why: The anterior forearm contains four superficial flexor-pronator muscles, one intermediate muscle and three deep muscles. The superficial and intermediate group crosses the elbow, whereas the deep group arises distal to it.

notes.A: There are eight muscles in total in the anterior compartment: four superficial, one intermediate and three deep.
notes.B: The superficial group arises in part near the medial epicondyle and extends across the elbow into the forearm.
notes.C: The deep flexor-pronator muscles arise from the forearm bones or interosseous membrane and do not cross the elbow joint.
notes.D: Pronator quadratus inserts on the distal radius rather than on the digits; only the two deep long flexors reach the digits.
notes.E: The anterior flexor compartment is generally more massive, reflecting the force needed to flex the fingers during gripping.

ana-gpq-62.why: The cubital fossa is a triangular depression anterior to the elbow, with brachialis and supinator forming its floor. The bicipital aponeurosis reinforces the roof rather than lying among its deep contents.

notes.A: The cubital fossa is triangular, with its base joining the epicondyles and its apex pointing distally.
notes.B: Pronator teres forms the medial border of the triangular space as it crosses the anterior forearm.
notes.C: Brachioradialis forms the lateral border, converging distally towards pronator teres at the apex.
notes.D: Brachialis forms the proximal floor and supinator contributes to the distal floor of the cubital fossa.
notes.E: The bicipital aponeurosis extends medially across the fossa as part of its roof, superficial to the brachial artery and median nerve.

ana-gpq-63.why: The deep anterior forearm group consists of flexor digitorum profundus, flexor pollicis longus and pronator quadratus. Their attachments allow flexion of the distal digits and pronation at the distal radioulnar joint.

notes.A: Pronator quadratus lies deep in the distal forearm, joining the ulna and radius to produce pronation.
notes.B: Flexor pollicis longus lies in the deep anterior compartment and flexes the interphalangeal joint of the thumb.
notes.C: Palmaris longus belongs to the superficial flexor group and tenses the palmar aponeurosis.
notes.D: Flexor digitorum profundus lies deep to superficialis and flexes the distal interphalangeal joints of the four fingers.
notes.E: Flexor digitorum superficialis forms the intermediate layer and inserts on the middle phalanges rather than the distal phalanges.

ana-gpq-64.why: The thumb’s outcropping muscles originate deep in the posterior forearm and emerge towards its radial side. Their tendons reach the thumb, in contrast to extensor indicis, which remains directed towards the index finger.

notes.A: Extensor indicis belongs to the deep extensor group but runs towards the index finger instead of outcropping towards the thumb.
notes.B: Extensor pollicis brevis emerges on the radial side and extends the thumb at its metacarpophalangeal joint.
notes.C: Extensor digitorum is a superficial extensor of the four fingers, rather than one of the deep thumb muscles.
notes.D: Abductor pollicis longus emerges radially with extensor pollicis brevis and abducts the thumb at its carpometacarpal joint.
notes.E: Extensor pollicis longus emerges from the deep group and turns around the dorsal radial tubercle towards the thumb.

ana-gpq-65.why: The anatomical snuffbox is a triangular depression between thumb tendons, with the radial styloid near its proximal end. The radial artery crosses its bony floor over the scaphoid and trapezium.

notes.A: The radial styloid is a palpable bony landmark near the proximal base of the anatomical snuffbox.
notes.B: Extensor pollicis longus forms the medial or ulnar border of the snuffbox, rather than its lateral border.
notes.C: Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis form the lateral or radial boundary rather than the medial boundary.
notes.D: Lister’s tubercle is the dorsal radial pulley around which extensor pollicis longus turns near the medial border.
notes.E: Extensor pollicis brevis travels with abductor pollicis longus to form the lateral border of the snuffbox.

ana-gpq-66.why: The flexor retinaculum forms the roof of the carpal tunnel, which carries the median nerve and nine long digital flexor tendons. Structures lying superficial to the retinaculum escape direct compression within the tunnel.

notes.A: The palmaris longus tendon passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum before blending with the palmar aponeurosis.
notes.B: Flexor pollicis longus passes through the carpal tunnel deep to the retinaculum on its way to the thumb.
notes.C: Flexor carpi ulnaris inserts on the pisiform and does not traverse the carpal tunnel beneath the retinaculum.
notes.D: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve travels superficial to the flexor retinaculum to supply the central palm.
notes.E: The median nerve passes through the carpal tunnel beneath the flexor retinaculum alongside the long flexor tendons.

ana-gpq-77.why: Fascia lata is the investing deep fascia of the thigh and forms the lateral iliotibial tract. It attaches to bony landmarks and has a saphenous opening for the great saphenous vein.

notes.A: Fascia lata invests the thigh muscles as deep fascia, lying beneath the subcutaneous tissue and superficial fascia.
notes.B: Scarpa’s fascia fuses with fascia lata just inferior to the inguinal ligament rather than continuing freely as the deep thigh fascia.
notes.C: The iliotibial tract is a lateral thickening of fascia lata extending towards the lateral tibial condyle.
notes.D: The fascia lata attaches around the knee to bony landmarks including the tibial condyles and fibular head.
notes.E: The great saphenous vein passes through the saphenous opening and its cribriform fascia to enter the femoral vein.

ana-gpq-78.why: The femoral triangle is a proximal anterior thigh region bounded by the inguinal ligament, sartorius and adductor longus. It contains major femoral vessels, the femoral nerve and lymphatic structures.

notes.A: The medial border of adductor longus forms the medial boundary and converges with sartorius at the distal apex.
notes.B: The base lies superiorly along the inguinal ligament, while the apex lies inferiorly at the beginning of the adductor canal.
notes.C: The medial border of sartorius forms the lateral boundary of the femoral triangle, not its lateral border.
notes.D: The inguinal ligament spans the anterior superior iliac spine and pubic tubercle and forms the base of the triangle.
notes.E: Deep inguinal lymph nodes lie in the femoral triangle, including the highest node near the femoral canal.

ana-gpq-80.why: The femoral sheath is a funnel-shaped fascial extension from the abdomen into the upper thigh. It encloses the femoral artery, vein and canal, but the femoral nerve remains outside it.

notes.A: Transversalis fascia extends inferiorly behind the inguinal ligament to form the anterior wall of the femoral sheath.
notes.B: Iliac fascia contributes the posterior wall of the sheath as it extends into the proximal thigh.
notes.C: Psoas fascia invests psoas major; the posterior contribution to the sheath is conventionally named iliac fascia.
notes.D: Pectineal fascia covers pectineus but is not one of the two principal fascial layers forming the femoral sheath.
notes.E: The inguinal ligament lies anterior to the femoral sheath as it enters the thigh but does not form the sheath itself.

ana-gpq-81.why: The femoral canal is the medial compartment of the femoral sheath, with a proximal opening called the femoral ring. Its relatively rigid boundaries explain why a femoral hernia may become strangulated.

notes.A: The femoral canal lies medial to the femoral vein, allowing some expansion of the vein within the sheath.
notes.B: The femoral ring is the proximal entrance to the femoral canal through which a femoral hernia may protrude.
notes.C: The inguinal ligament forms the anterior boundary of the femoral ring, with the lacunar ligament lying medially.
notes.D: The canal contains loose connective tissue, fat, lymphatics and commonly the highest deep inguinal node of Cloquet.
notes.E: The lacunar ligament forms the medial boundary of the ring and may be divided surgically, with care to avoid variant vessels.

ana-gpq-83.why: The adductor canal connects the femoral triangle to the adductor hiatus and transmits femoral vessels along the medial thigh. The saphenous nerve leaves the canal before the vessels enter the popliteal fossa.

notes.A: Hunter’s canal and the subsartorial canal are alternative names for the adductor canal in the medial thigh.
notes.B: Sartorius overlies a fascial roof that separates the canal’s contents from the superficial tissues of the medial thigh.
notes.C: Adductor longus proximally and adductor magnus distally form the posterior or posteromedial wall of the canal.
notes.D: The nerve to vastus lateralis supplies the lateral quadriceps and is not a conventional content of the adductor canal.
notes.E: The saphenous nerve accompanies the femoral vessels through much of the canal before emerging medially towards the leg.

ana-gpq-89.why: The popliteal fossa is a diamond-shaped space posterior to the knee. Its principal neurovascular structures are arranged from superficial to deep as tibial nerve, popliteal vein and popliteal artery.

notes.A: Biceps femoris forms the superolateral boundary, while semimembranosus and semitendinosus form the superomedial boundary of the fossa.
notes.B: The popliteal fascia is the deep fascial continuation of fascia lata and forms the deep component of the roof.
notes.C: The floor also includes the posterior knee capsule and popliteus muscle, in addition to the popliteal surface of the femur.
notes.D: The popliteal artery lies deepest in the central neurovascular bundle, close to the femur and posterior knee capsule.
notes.E: The small saphenous vein usually pierces the popliteal fascia to terminate in the popliteal vein.

ana-gpq-91.why: The deep fibular nerve supplies the anterior leg compartment, whose muscles dorsiflex the ankle or extend the toes. Fibularis tertius also everts the foot and travels with the long toe extensors.

notes.A: Tibialis posterior occupies the deep posterior compartment and plantarflexes and inverts the foot.
notes.B: Fibularis longus runs in the lateral compartment, where its tendon helps evert the foot and assists plantarflexion.
notes.C: Extensor digitorum longus lies anteriorly and extends the lateral four toes while assisting ankle dorsiflexion.
notes.D: Extensor digitorum brevis is an intrinsic muscle on the dorsum of the foot, not a muscle of the leg.
notes.E: Fibularis tertius lies in the anterior compartment and assists dorsiflexion and eversion of the foot.

ana-gpq-93.why: The deep posterior leg muscles comprise popliteus, tibialis posterior and the two long toe flexors. The tibial nerve supplies this group, which lies deep to soleus and gastrocnemius.

notes.A: Flexor digitorum longus occupies the deep posterior compartment and flexes the distal phalanges of the lateral four toes.
notes.B: Flexor hallucis longus lies in the deep posterior compartment and provides powerful great toe flexion during push-off.
notes.C: Soleus lies in the superficial posterior compartment and joins gastrocnemius to form the calcaneal tendon.
notes.D: Tibialis posterior occupies the deep posterior compartment and supports the medial longitudinal arch while inverting the foot.
notes.E: Extensor hallucis longus occupies the anterior compartment and extends the great toe rather than flexing it.

ana-gpq-94.why: The first plantar muscle layer lies immediately deep to the plantar aponeurosis. It consists of abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis and abductor digiti minimi; the long flexor tendons and their associated muscles lie deeper.

notes.A: The flexor digitorum longus tendon divides into four digital tendons in the second plantar layer.
notes.B: The lumbricals arise from the flexor digitorum longus tendons in the second plantar layer.
notes.C: Abductor hallucis occupies the medial side of the superficial plantar layer and abducts the great toe.
notes.D: Abductor digiti minimi occupies the lateral side of the first plantar layer and acts on the fifth toe.
notes.E: Quadratus plantae lies in the second layer and assists the long flexor tendons in pulling the toes directly backwards.

ana-gpq-128.why: The deep inguinal ring lies lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and transmits the spermatic cord or round ligament. This vascular relationship distinguishes indirect from direct inguinal hernias.

notes.A: The inferior epigastric vessels ascend just medial to the deep inguinal ring and mark the lateral boundary of Hesselbach’s triangle.
notes.B: The ductus deferens curves around the lateral side of the inferior epigastric artery to reach the deep inguinal ring.
notes.C: The round ligament enters the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric artery, just as the ductus deferens does.
notes.D: An indirect inguinal hernia enters the deep ring, placing its neck lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.
notes.E: The superficial inguinal ring lies immediately above and medial to the pubic tubercle, unlike the femoral canal.

ana-osa-54.why: An indirect inguinal hernia enters the canal through the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. Weakness of the posterior wall near the conjoint tendon instead permits a direct hernia.

notes.A: A persistent processus vaginalis provides a congenital pathway along which abdominal contents can enter the inguinal canal.
notes.C: The neck of an indirect hernia lies lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels because it enters through the deep ring.
notes.D: An indirect sac can traverse the entire inguinal canal and emerge at the superficial ring above and medial to the pubic tubercle.
notes.E: The indirect route allows the sac to descend along the spermatic cord into the scrotum or towards the labium majus.

ana-osa-55.why: The pubic tubercle provides a reliable surface landmark: an inguinal hernia emerging through the superficial ring lies superomedial to it, whereas a femoral hernia neck lies inferolateral.

notes.A: Hernia size varies with the sac and its contents, so relative size does not reliably identify the anatomical route.
notes.B: A femoral hernia can produce a visible swelling in the groin or upper thigh below the inguinal ligament.
notes.C: A femoral hernia passes beneath the inguinal ligament, so its neck lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
notes.E: Femoral hernias occur more commonly in women than men; sex alone is not a reliable anatomical distinction.

ana-g16-a5.why: Teres minor inserts on the inferior facet of the greater tubercle. The intertubercular groove and its lips provide separate attachment sites for latissimus dorsi, pectoralis major and teres major.

notes.A: Teres minor is a rotator cuff muscle that inserts on the greater tubercle rather than within the intertubercular groove.

ana-g16-a10.why: In the conventional count, five anterior forearm muscles have medial epicondylar attachments, whereas six muscles attach to the lateral epicondyle. The lateral supracondylar ridge is a separate attachment site.

notes.A: The medial epicondyle is a shared flexor attachment, while the lateral epicondyle gives origin to the common extensors and other muscles.

ana-g16-a12.why: Latissimus dorsi connects the pelvis to the upper limb through attachments to the posterior iliac crest and the floor of the humeral intertubercular groove. It transmits force between the trunk and humerus.

notes.B: Latissimus dorsi has an iliac crest attachment, distinguishing it from the other conventional muscles connecting the upper limb to the axial skeleton.

ana-g16-a13.why: The triangle of auscultation enlarges when the scapulae are protracted, such as when a person folds the arms and leans forward. This exposes a relatively thin muscular window over the posterior thorax.

notes.A: Retracting the scapulae moves their medial borders towards the vertebral column and reduces the available auscultatory window.

ana-g16-a17.why: The superolateral border of the popliteal fossa is formed by biceps femoris. Semimembranosus and semitendinosus instead form the superomedial border, reflecting their position on the medial posterior thigh.

notes.A: Semimembranosus and semitendinosus pass along the medial side of the knee and therefore form the superomedial boundary.

ana-g16-a20.why: Psoas major and iliacus converge below the inguinal ligament as iliopsoas, inserting principally on the lesser trochanter of the femur. This anterior line of pull makes iliopsoas a powerful hip flexor.

notes.B: The lesser trochanter is the principal insertion of iliopsoas, whereas the greater trochanter receives several hip abductor and rotator tendons.

ana-g16-a22.why: Extensor hallucis longus belongs to the anterior compartment and is supplied by the deep fibular nerve. The deep posterior compartment instead contains the long toe flexors, tibialis posterior and popliteus.

notes.A: Extensor hallucis longus crosses the anterior ankle to extend the great toe and assist dorsiflexion, not posterior compartment plantarflexion.

ana-g16-a24.why: The adductor (subsartorial) canal runs from the apex of the femoral triangle to the adductor hiatus, where the femoral vessels pass into the popliteal fossa.

notes.B: The adductor canal begins where sartorius crosses adductor longus and ends at the opening in adductor magnus.

ana-g16-a25.why: The lacunar ligament forms the medial boundary of the femoral ring by reflecting from the medial end of the inguinal ligament towards the pecten pubis. The femoral vein lies lateral to the ring.

notes.B: The medial edge of the ring is the lacunar ligament, whereas the pectineal ligament forms its posterior boundary.

ana-g16-a26.why: The inguinal ligament is the thickened inferior margin of the external oblique aponeurosis, extending from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle. The symphysis lies further medially.

notes.A: The pubic tubercle is the medial attachment of the inguinal ligament, whereas the pubic symphysis is the midline joint between the pubic bones.

ana-g16-a32.why: The membranous superficial fascia of the abdomen is continuous with the superficial fascia of the external genitalia and Colles’ fascia in the perineum. These continuities explain the spread of urine after spongy urethral rupture.

notes.B: The superficial fascial layers of the penis, scrotum and perineum are continuous with Scarpa’s fascia, although their local structure and names differ.

ana-g16-a43.why: The right diaphragmatic crus is usually longer and broader than the left. It typically attaches to the upper three lumbar vertebral bodies, whereas the left crus attaches to the upper two.

notes.B: The right crus generally extends inferiorly to the third lumbar vertebra, whereas the left usually extends to the second.

ana-g16-a44.why: The caval opening is in the central tendon of the diaphragm at approximately T8, allowing the inferior vena cava to reach the right atrium. The oesophageal hiatus lies at T10 and the aortic hiatus at T12.

notes.A: T10 is the conventional level of the oesophageal hiatus, while the inferior vena cava traverses the central tendon at T8.

ana-g16-a46.why: The interosseous portions of the internal intercostals principally depress the ribs during active expiration. Their interchondral portions can elevate the ribs during inspiration, so the two portions have different mechanical effects.

notes.A: The interosseous internal intercostals mainly assist forced expiration, although the interchondral fibres can contribute to inspiration.

ana-g16-a47.why: Intercostal muscle activity stabilises the chest wall against pressure differences during breathing, limiting inward bulging of intercostal spaces during inspiration. These muscles also contribute to rib movement and changes in thoracic volume.

notes.B: The intercostals reinforce the spaces between adjacent ribs, resisting deformation while the diaphragm changes intrathoracic pressure.

ana-g16-a48.why: Abdominal muscle contraction increases intra-abdominal pressure and displaces the relaxed diaphragm upwards during forced expiration. This reduces thoracic volume rather than producing the downward diaphragmatic movement needed for inspiration.

notes.A: Abdominal muscles mainly assist active expiration by compressing the abdominal contents and pushing the diaphragm superiorly.

ana-g16-a126.why: The perineal body is a fibromuscular node between the anal canal and the urogenital structures where several perineal muscles converge; tearing it weakens the pelvic floor.

notes.A: Fibres of the external anal sphincter blend with the perineal body anterior to the anal canal.
notes.B: Pubovaginalis is a medial component of levator ani whose fibres contribute to the perineal body in females.
notes.C: Levator prostatae is the male counterpart of pubovaginalis and contributes fibres to the perineal body.
notes.D: Bulbospongiosus attaches to the perineal body and contributes to the convergence of superficial perineal muscles.
notes.E: The deep transverse perineal muscle contributes to stabilisation of the perineal body through its medial attachment.

ana-g16-a161.why: The femoral ring opens into the medial compartment of the femoral sheath. Its boundaries are clinically important because a femoral hernia may become strangulated at the rigid ring, near an aberrant obturator vessel.

notes.A: The lacunar ligament forms the medial boundary of the ring, whereas the femoral vein lies laterally.
notes.B: The pectineal ligament lies along the superior pubic ramus and contributes to the posterior boundary of the femoral ring.
notes.C: The inguinal ligament forms the anterior boundary of the ring, separating it from the abdominal wall above.
notes.D: An aberrant obturator artery can pass close to the lacunar ligament, creating a risk of bleeding during hernia surgery.
notes.E: The node of Cloquet is the highest deep inguinal lymph node and may occupy the upper part of the femoral canal.

ana-g16-a171.why: A subumbilical midline incision traverses the anterior abdominal wall through its superficial fascia and linea alba before reaching the extraperitoneal tissue and parietal peritoneum. It avoids cutting the rectus muscle bellies.

notes.A: Scarpa’s fascia is the membranous layer of the superficial fascia and lies deep to the fatty layer below the umbilicus.
notes.B: The linea alba is the midline fusion of abdominal muscle aponeuroses, providing a relatively avascular surgical plane.
notes.C: Fascia iliaca covers iliacus on the posterior abdominal wall, rather than forming part of the anterior midline incision path.
notes.D: Extraperitoneal fat lies between the transversalis fascia and parietal peritoneum and is encountered before entering the peritoneal cavity.
notes.E: Parietal peritoneum lines the abdominal wall and is opened; visceral peritoneum covers the abdominal organs instead.

ana-g16-a176.why: An indirect inguinal hernia enters the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and follows the inguinal canal. It can descend into the scrotum along the spermatic cord.

notes.A: Entry through the deep inguinal ring is the defining anatomical route of an indirect inguinal hernia.
notes.B: A hernia neck medial to the inferior epigastric vessels indicates a direct hernia through the posterior wall of the canal.
notes.C: An inguinoscrotal swelling following the canal strongly supports an indirect route, although direct hernias may rarely reach the scrotum.
notes.D: Bowel may occupy either type of inguinal hernia sac, so intestinal contents do not establish its anatomical route.

ana-g16-a181.why: A direct inguinal hernia protrudes through the weakened posterior inguinal wall within Hesselbach’s triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. It bypasses the deep ring and rarely descends into the scrotum.

notes.A: A sac lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels enters the deep ring and is classified as an indirect hernia.
notes.B: Hesselbach’s triangle is the area of the posterior inguinal wall through which direct hernias typically protrude.
notes.C: Both direct and indirect hernias may contain loops of bowel, depending on what enters the sac.
notes.D: A direct sac may emerge through the superficial ring after entering the canal through its posterior wall rather than the deep ring.
notes.E: The direct route usually produces a medial groin bulge and only rarely extends far enough to enter the scrotum.

ana-g16-a186.why: Small bowel and greater omentum are common mobile intra-abdominal contents of an inguinoscrotal hernia. Fixed retroperitoneal structures are less typical, and fluid within the tunica vaginalis is a hydrocele.

notes.A: Mobile loops of small intestine can enter a patent inguinal pathway and descend within the peritoneal hernia sac.
notes.B: The greater omentum is a mobile peritoneal fold that can protrude into an indirect inguinal hernia sac.
notes.C: The ascending colon is usually secondarily retroperitoneal and is an uncommon hernia content, although sliding hernias can involve it.
notes.D: A bladder protrusion through Hesselbach’s triangle follows a direct route rather than the described indirect inguinoscrotal route.
notes.E: Fluid collecting between the layers of the tunica vaginalis constitutes a hydrocele, not protruding abdominal contents.

ana-g16-c1.why: The cervical sympathetic trunk descends on the prevertebral muscles, immediately behind the carotid sheath. Unlike the vagus, it is not a principal content of the sheath.

notes.A: The superior root of the ansa cervicalis is usually on the anterior surface of the carotid sheath as it descends towards the infrahyoid muscles.
notes.B: The trachea is a midline visceral structure lying medial to the carotid sheath rather than directly posterior to it.
notes.D: The internal jugular vein is a principal content of the sheath, lying lateral to the carotid artery.
notes.E: The vagus is a content of the sheath and usually lies posteriorly between the carotid artery and internal jugular vein.

ana-g16-c2.why: The orbital plate of the frontal bone forms most of the orbital roof, which separates the orbit from the anterior cranial fossa; the lesser wing of the sphenoid completes it posteriorly.

notes.A: The orbital process of the palatine bone forms a small posterior part of the orbital floor near the inferior orbital fissure.
notes.B: The orbital surface of the maxilla forms most of the floor separating the orbit from the maxillary sinus.
notes.D: The zygomatic bone forms parts of the lateral wall and floor, where the two surfaces meet anterolaterally.
notes.E: The lacrimal bone forms part of the anterior medial orbital wall and helps enclose the lacrimal sac.

ana-g16-c3.why: The common carotid artery normally divides into internal and external carotid arteries near the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, approximately at C4, within the carotid triangle.

notes.A: The carotid triangle contains the bifurcation, but C7 is substantially below its usual level near the thyroid cartilage.
notes.C: The submental triangle lies beneath the chin between the anterior digastric bellies and does not contain the carotid bifurcation.
notes.D: Although bifurcation height varies, the submental triangle is a midline region unrelated to the usual site of carotid division.
notes.E: The muscular triangle contains the infrahyoid muscles and cervical viscera; the carotid bifurcation usually lies in the carotid triangle.

ana-g16-c8.why: The maxillary sinus drains through an opening high on its medial wall into the hiatus semilunaris of the middle nasal meatus, making gravity-dependent drainage relatively inefficient.

notes.A: The frontal sinus drains through the frontal recess into the middle meatus rather than the superior meatus.
notes.B: Anterior ethmoidal cells drain into the middle meatus, whereas posterior ethmoidal cells drain into the superior meatus.
notes.D: The nasolacrimal duct carries tears from the lacrimal sac into the inferior meatus, not secretions from the sphenoidal sinus.
notes.E: The sphenoethmoidal recess lies above the superior concha and receives drainage from the sphenoidal sinus.

ana-g16-c9.why: The inferior orbital fissure provides a communication between the posterior orbit and the pterygopalatine fossa medially, allowing passage of branches of the maxillary nerve and accompanying vessels.

notes.A: The pterygoid canal connects the pterygopalatine fossa with the region of the foramen lacerum and transmits the Vidian nerve.
notes.B: The infratemporal fossa is a neighbouring space; the actual orbital communication is through the inferior orbital fissure.
notes.D: The superior orbital fissure connects the orbit with the middle cranial fossa and transmits several ocular nerves.
notes.E: The optic canal connects the orbit with the cranial cavity and transmits the optic nerve and ophthalmic artery.

ana-g16-c10.why: Both divisions of the oculomotor nerve pass through the superior orbital fissure inside the common tendinous ring, together with the nasociliary and abducent nerves.

notes.B: The trochlear nerve passes through the superior orbital fissure outside the ring to reach the superior oblique muscle.
notes.C: The ophthalmic artery passes through the optic canal with the optic nerve, separate from the superior orbital fissure.
notes.D: The superior ophthalmic vein usually traverses the superior orbital fissure outside the common tendinous ring to reach the cavernous sinus.
notes.E: The lacrimal nerve passes through the superior orbital fissure outside the ring before running along the lateral orbital wall.

ana-g16-c13.why: A communicating branch of the inferior ophthalmic vein can pass through the inferior orbital fissure to the pterygoid venous plexus, providing a route between orbital and infratemporal veins.

notes.A: The oculomotor nerve enters through the superior orbital fissure within the tendinous ring, not the inferior fissure.
notes.B: The trochlear nerve enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure outside the common tendinous ring.
notes.C: The optic canal carries the ophthalmic artery into the orbit alongside the optic nerve.
notes.D: The lacrimal nerve is an ophthalmic division branch entering through the superior orbital fissure outside the tendinous ring.

ana-g16-c14.why: The greater petrosal nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibres from the facial nerve and joins the deep petrosal nerve carrying postganglionic sympathetic fibres to form the Vidian nerve.

notes.A: The deep petrosal nerve contributes sympathetic fibres, but the lesser petrosal nerve carries parasympathetic fibres towards the otic ganglion.
notes.C: The greater petrosal nerve supplies the parasympathetic component, but the lesser petrosal nerve carries fibres to the otic ganglion.
notes.D: The tympanic nerve contributes to the tympanic plexus, from which the lesser petrosal nerve carries fibres towards the otic ganglion.
notes.E: The lesser petrosal nerve supplies the otic ganglion pathway and does not unite with the deep petrosal nerve to form the Vidian nerve.

ana-g16-c15.why: The posterior wall of the maxillary sinus provides surgical access to the pterygopalatine fossa, where the Vidian nerve and terminal maxillary artery can be approached for selected procedures.

notes.A: The frontal sinus is accessed through its frontal drainage pathway or a dedicated frontal approach, rather than through the pterygopalatine fossa.
notes.B: Upper molar teeth are removed through the oral cavity; their proximity to the maxillary sinus does not require entering the pterygopalatine fossa.
notes.D: The cavernous sinus is an intracranial venous space and is not the usual target of a transantral pterygopalatine approach.
notes.E: The nasolacrimal duct runs anteriorly from the lacrimal sac to the inferior nasal meatus, outside the pterygopalatine fossa.

ana-g16-c16.why: The lacrimal gland occupies a shallow depression in the orbital plate of the frontal bone at the superolateral orbit. Its ducts release tears into the superior conjunctival fornix.

notes.A: The inferolateral orbit is near the zygomatic contribution to the orbital floor; the lacrimal gland occupies the superior lateral region.
notes.B: The superomedial orbit contains the trochlea of superior oblique, whereas the lacrimal gland is situated on the lateral side.
notes.C: The lateral orbital floor is formed partly by zygomatic bone and lies below the normal location of the lacrimal gland.
notes.E: The superior orbital fissure is a posterior passage for nerves and veins, not the anterior superolateral lacrimal gland fossa.

ana-g16-c19.why: The palatine processes of the paired maxillae form the anterior portion of the hard palate, while the horizontal plates of the palatine bones complete its posterior part.

notes.A: The sphenoid contributes to the skull base and the zygomatic bone to the cheek and orbit; neither forms the hard palate.
notes.B: The maxilla contributes its palatine process, but the frontal bone forms the forehead and orbital roof rather than the palate.
notes.C: The ethmoid and frontal bones contribute to nasal and orbital structures but do not form the bony roof of the mouth.
notes.E: The palatine bone forms the posterior hard palate through its horizontal plate, while the ethmoid forms nasal and orbital structures.

ana-g16-c23.why: Inferior oblique originates anteriorly from the maxillary orbital floor near the nasolacrimal canal, unlike the four rectus muscles, which originate from the common tendinous ring at the orbital apex.

notes.B: Medial rectus originates from the common tendinous ring and inserts on the medial sclera to adduct the eyeball.
notes.C: Lateral rectus originates from the common tendinous ring and abducts the eyeball under abducent nerve control.
notes.D: Inferior rectus originates from the common tendinous ring and primarily depresses the eyeball, with additional adduction and extorsion.
notes.E: The four rectus muscles share the tendinous ring, but inferior oblique has a separate origin on the anterior orbital floor.

ana-g16-c26.why: The phrenic nerve descends on the anterior scalene muscle beneath the prevertebral fascial covering, outside the carotid sheath, which encloses the carotid artery, internal jugular vein and vagus.

notes.A: The common carotid artery is enclosed medially within the sheath before dividing into its internal and external branches.
notes.B: The internal jugular vein lies inside the carotid sheath, usually lateral to the common or internal carotid artery.
notes.C: The vagus nerve is enclosed in the sheath posteriorly between the carotid artery and internal jugular vein.
notes.E: Deep cervical lymph nodes lie along the internal jugular vein and may be embedded in or closely associated with the sheath.

ana-g16-c29.why: The palatine tonsil occupies the tonsillar fossa in the lateral oropharyngeal wall between the palatoglossal arch anteriorly and palatopharyngeal arch posteriorly, formed by their corresponding muscles.

notes.A: Palatoglossus forms the anterior tonsillar pillar, but styloglossus retracts the tongue and does not form the posterior pillar.
notes.B: The superior constrictor contributes to the tonsillar bed, while stylopharyngeus elevates the pharynx; neither pair defines the tonsillar pillars.
notes.C: Stylopharyngeus elevates the pharynx and styloglossus retracts the tongue, but neither forms the arches enclosing the tonsil.
notes.E: Palatoglossus forms the anterior arch, whereas stylopharyngeus runs deeper and does not form the posterior tonsillar arch.

ana-g16-c35.why: Most salivary stones occur in the submandibular gland or its duct. Proposed contributors include relatively viscous saliva and a long duct that carries secretions forward and upwards to the floor of the mouth.

notes.A: The parotid gland secretes predominantly watery serous saliva and develops calculi less frequently than the submandibular gland.
notes.C: The sublingual gland drains through multiple short ducts and is an uncommon site of salivary stone formation.
notes.D: The lacrimal gland produces tears rather than saliva, so it is not a site of sialolithiasis.
notes.E: Submandibular stones are much more frequent. The longer duct and more viscous secretion are proposed contributors to this difference.

ana-g16-c36.why: The lacrimal sac sits in the lacrimal sac fossa on the anterior medial orbital wall near the medial canthus. It drains through the nasolacrimal duct into the inferior nasal meatus.

notes.A: The orbital floor separates the orbit from the maxillary sinus, but the sac occupies the anterior medial orbital wall.
notes.B: The inferolateral orbit is remote from the medial canthus where the lacrimal canaliculi enter the lacrimal sac.
notes.C: The sac lies anteriorly near the medial canthus rather than high on the superomedial orbital wall.
notes.E: The nasolacrimal duct carries tears beneath the inferior concha to the inferior meatus, below the stated drainage site.

ana-g16-c37.why: The sphenopalatine foramen in the medial boundary of the pterygopalatine fossa leads into the nasal cavity, transmitting the sphenopalatine vessels and posterior superior nasal nerve branches.

notes.A: The nasolacrimal duct connects the lacrimal sac with the inferior nasal meatus rather than the pterygopalatine fossa.
notes.B: The inferior meatus receives the nasolacrimal duct but is not the opening connecting the pterygopalatine fossa to the nose.
notes.D: The superior orbital fissure connects the middle cranial fossa and orbit, not the pterygopalatine fossa and nasal cavity.
notes.E: The infraorbital foramen carries the infraorbital nerve and vessels to the face through the anterior surface of the maxilla.

ana-g16-c42.why: The perpendicular plate of the palatine bone forms the medial wall of the pterygopalatine fossa; the sphenopalatine foramen interrupts this wall to provide access to the nasal cavity.

notes.A: The greater wing of the sphenoid contributes to the superior or posterior boundary rather than forming the medial wall.
notes.B: The lateral pterygoid plate is part of the sphenoid process, whose root contributes to the posterior aspect of the fossa.
notes.C: The medial pterygoid plate is part of the sphenoid pterygoid process; the medial fossa wall is formed by palatine bone.
notes.D: The posterior surface of the maxilla forms the anterior boundary of the fossa rather than its medial wall.

ana-g16-c44.why: Lateral cricoarytenoid pulls the muscular processes of the arytenoids anterolaterally, rotating their vocal processes medially and closing the membranous portion of the rima glottidis during phonation.

notes.A: Transverse arytenoid draws the arytenoid cartilages together to close the posterior glottis, rather than primarily rotating their muscular processes.
notes.B: Posterior cricoarytenoid rotates the vocal processes laterally and is the only intrinsic muscle that abducts the vocal folds.
notes.D: Thyroarytenoid shortens and relaxes the vocal ligaments, modifying their tension rather than providing the described rotational action.
notes.E: Aryepiglottic muscle narrows the laryngeal inlet during swallowing rather than primarily adducting the vocal folds.

ana-g16-n70.why: The jugular foramen transmits the glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory nerves, together with venous drainage including the sigmoid sinus continuing as the internal jugular vein. The hypoglossal nerve uses a separate canal.

notes.A: The foramen transmits cranial nerves as well as the venous channel formed by the continuation of the sigmoid sinus.
notes.B: The vagus passes through the foramen with the glossopharyngeal and accessory nerves, alongside major venous drainage.
notes.C: The hypoglossal nerve leaves through a canal in the occipital bone that is separate from the jugular foramen.
notes.D: This combination includes the hypoglossal nerve, which uses its own canal and does not traverse the jugular foramen.

ana-ms15-6.why: The soft palate is a mobile fibromuscular continuation of the hard palate. It regulates communication between the nasopharynx and oropharynx during swallowing and speech, while its free posterior margin bears the uvula.

notes.A: Its anterior palatine aponeurosis attaches to the posterior margin of the bony hard palate.
notes.B: The soft palate forms the superior boundary of the oropharyngeal isthmus, connecting the mouth to the pharynx.
notes.C: The palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal folds descend from its lateral margins around the tonsillar fossa.
notes.D: The soft palate elevates transiently during swallowing to close the nasopharynx, not the oropharynx continuously.
notes.E: The posterior margin hangs freely into the pharynx and bears the centrally placed uvula.

ana-ms15-7.why: Waldeyer’s lymphatic ring surrounds the entrance to the respiratory and digestive tracts. Its palatine and lingual components are associated with the oropharynx, while the tubal and pharyngeal components occupy the nasopharynx.

notes.A: The lingual tonsil consists of lymphoid nodules on the posterior third of the tongue facing the oropharynx.
notes.B: The tubal tonsil surrounds the pharyngeal opening of the auditory tube in the lateral nasopharynx.
notes.C: The palatine tonsil occupies the lateral oropharyngeal wall between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches.
notes.D: The pharyngeal tonsil occupies the roof and posterior wall of the nasopharynx rather than the oropharynx.

ana-ms15-40.why: The pharyngeal wall consists of mucosa, pharyngobasilar fascia, skeletal muscle and external buccopharyngeal fascia. The prevertebral fascia lies outside this wall, covering the deep vertebral muscles.

notes.A: The mucous membrane lines the pharyngeal lumen and provides epithelial protection appropriate to its respiratory or digestive region.
notes.B: The pharyngobasilar fascia provides a fibrous supporting layer deep to the mucosa and attaches to the skull base.
notes.C: The constrictors and longitudinal pharyngeal muscles are skeletal muscles that propel food and elevate the pharynx during swallowing.
notes.D: The buccopharyngeal fascia is the external covering of the constrictors and extends forwards over the buccinator.

ana-gpq-12.why: Cervical fascial spaces provide pathways for infection. The retropharyngeal space communicates laterally with parapharyngeal regions, while the sublingual and submandibular spaces communicate around the posterior border of mylohyoid.

notes.A: The prevertebral space lies deep to the prevertebral fascia in relation to the vertebral column and deep muscles.
notes.B: The retropharyngeal space is anterior to the prevertebral fascia, with the alar fascia forming its more immediate posterior boundary.
notes.C: The parapharyngeal and retropharyngeal spaces communicate, allowing infections in the lateral pharyngeal region to spread posteriorly.
notes.D: The parapharyngeal space extends to the skull base but is anatomically distinct from the more lateral infratemporal fossa.
notes.E: The submandibular and sublingual spaces communicate behind mylohyoid, permitting infection to spread between the two regions.

ana-gpq-13.why: The superficial cervical fascia contains platysma and cutaneous nerves that emerge near the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid. Deeper motor nerves and cervical plexus loops lie beneath the investing fascia.

notes.A: The transverse cervical nerve runs superficially across sternocleidomastoid to supply the skin of the anterior neck.
notes.B: Platysma lies within the superficial fascia and tenses the skin of the neck during facial expression.
notes.C: The supraclavicular nerves descend in the superficial fascia towards the skin covering the clavicle and shoulder.
notes.D: The suprascapular nerve is a brachial plexus branch that courses deeply towards the scapular notch.
notes.E: The ansa cervicalis lies deep to the investing fascia, commonly on the anterior surface of the carotid sheath.

ana-gpq-14.why: Extrinsic tongue muscles originate outside the tongue and enter it to change its position. Intrinsic muscles instead arise and insert within the tongue, altering its shape.

notes.A: Genioglossus originates from the superior mental spine of the mandible and protrudes the tongue.
notes.B: The vertical muscle is intrinsic to the tongue and flattens and broadens it during contraction.
notes.C: Mylohyoid arises from the mandible and forms the muscular floor of the mouth rather than entering the tongue.
notes.D: Styloglossus arises from the styloid process and retracts and elevates the tongue during swallowing.
notes.E: Palatoglossus originates from the palatine aponeurosis and elevates the posterior tongue towards the soft palate.

ana-gpq-20.why: Superior constrictor arises from the pterygoid region, pterygomandibular raphe and posterior mylohyoid line. Its fibres converge posteriorly towards the median pharyngeal raphe and pharyngeal tubercle.

notes.A: The pharyngeal tubercle anchors the upper end of the posterior raphe and is associated with insertion, not origin.
notes.B: The pterygoid hamulus provides an upper attachment for fibres of the superior pharyngeal constrictor.
notes.C: The lower part of the medial pterygoid plate contributes to the superior constrictor’s origin.
notes.D: The pterygomandibular raphe anchors the superior constrictor posteriorly and buccinator anteriorly, linking pharynx and cheek.
notes.E: The posterior part of the mylohyoid line provides a mandibular origin for fibres of the superior constrictor.

ana-gpq-21.why: The gap between the superior and middle pharyngeal constrictors allows the stylopharyngeus muscle and glossopharyngeal nerve to enter the pharyngeal wall, linking its longitudinal musculature with its sensory and motor supply.

notes.A: Stylopharyngeus descends from the styloid process and enters between the superior and middle constrictors to elevate the pharynx.
notes.B: Styloglossus passes towards the tongue to retract it and does not enter the pharyngeal wall through this gap.
notes.C: Salpingopharyngeus descends from the auditory tube region within the pharyngeal wall rather than traversing this lateral gap.
notes.D: Palatopharyngeus descends from the soft palate within the pharyngeal wall and does not enter through this gap.
notes.E: The glossopharyngeal nerve accompanies stylopharyngeus through the gap and provides pharyngeal sensory and stylopharyngeal motor innervation.

ana-gpq-22.why: The middle constrictor originates from both horns of the hyoid and the lower stylohyoid ligament. Its fibres fan posteriorly to the median pharyngeal raphe and constrict the pharynx during swallowing.

notes.A: The inferior portion of the stylohyoid ligament gives attachment to fibres of the middle pharyngeal constrictor.
notes.B: The thyrohyoid membrane spans the hyoid and thyroid cartilage but is not an origin of the middle constrictor.
notes.C: The greater horn of the hyoid provides an attachment for the middle constrictor’s broad muscular origin.
notes.D: The lesser horn of the hyoid provides an additional origin near the attachment of the stylohyoid ligament.
notes.E: The median pharyngeal raphe is where the constrictor fibres insert posteriorly, rather than where they originate.

ana-gpq-24.why: Killian's dehiscence is a weak posterior area between the oblique thyropharyngeus and transverse cricopharyngeus fibres of the inferior constrictor. Increased intraluminal pressure may force mucosa and submucosa through it.

notes.A: The two portions of the inferior constrictor meet at the weak area.
notes.B: The superior and inferior constrictors are separated by the middle constrictor, not by this dehiscence.
notes.C: Palatopharyngeus and stylopharyngeus are longitudinal muscles, not the margins of Killian's dehiscence.
notes.D: The weak area lies in the posterior pharyngeal wall, where a pouch can protrude.
notes.E: A Zenker diverticulum is a pulsion pouch that protrudes through this weak area.

ana-gpq-25.why: The nasopharynx lies behind the nasal cavity and above the soft palate. Its lateral walls contain the auditory tube openings, while its roof and posterior wall contain pharyngeal lymphoid tissue.

notes.A: The pharyngeal recess lies posterior to the elevation formed by the auditory tube.
notes.B: The pharyngeal opening of the auditory tube lies on the lateral nasopharyngeal wall.
notes.C: The pharyngeal tonsil occupies the roof and posterior wall of the nasopharynx.
notes.D: The palatine tonsil occupies the tonsillar fossa in the lateral wall of the oropharynx.
notes.E: The palatopharyngeal arch descends from the soft palate into the oropharynx.

ana-gpq-27.why: The soft-palate muscles coordinate tension and movement during swallowing and speech. Tensor veli palatini receives motor fibres from the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, while the others receive vagal fibres through the pharyngeal plexus.

notes.A: Tensor veli palatini tenses the palate and assists opening of the auditory tube.
notes.B: Levator veli palatini raises the soft palate to help close the nasopharynx during swallowing.
notes.C: Palatoglossus elevates the posterior tongue and narrows the oropharyngeal isthmus.
notes.D: Palatopharyngeus elevates the pharynx during swallowing and helps position the soft palate.
notes.E: Musculus uvulae shortens and elevates the uvula, helping seal the nasopharynx.

ana-gpq-28.why: The palatine tonsil receives multiple arterial branches, principally the tonsillar branch of the facial artery. Its extensive blood supply and nearby veins explain the risk of bleeding during tonsillectomy.

notes.A: The facial artery supplies the tonsil through its tonsillar and ascending palatine branches.
notes.B: The descending palatine branch of the maxillary artery contributes through its lesser palatine branches.
notes.C: Dorsal lingual branches reach the inferior part of the palatine tonsil.
notes.D: The internal carotid artery gives no cervical branches, although its proximity makes accidental injury dangerous.
notes.E: The ascending pharyngeal artery contributes small branches to the pharyngeal wall and tonsil.

ana-gpq-31.why: The adult larynx typically spans C3–C6, although its position varies with age and swallowing. The thyroid cartilage forms its anterior prominence and attaches superiorly to the hyoid by the thyrohyoid membrane.

notes.A: The superior extent of the adult larynx is approximately at the third cervical vertebra.
notes.B: The carotid bifurcation usually lies near the superior border of the thyroid cartilage, close to the upper larynx.
notes.C: The inferior border of the cricoid cartilage marks the transition to the trachea at about C6.
notes.D: The thyrohyoid membrane connects the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone, not the cricoid cartilage.
notes.E: The superior thyroid notch lies immediately above the laryngeal prominence in the anterior midline.

ana-osa-b12.why: The nasolacrimal duct carries tears from the lacrimal sac to the inferior nasal meatus beneath the inferior concha. This connection explains nasal discharge during crying.

notes.A: The middle meatus receives drainage from the frontal, maxillary and anterior or middle ethmoidal sinuses, rather than tears.
notes.B: The superior meatus receives posterior ethmoidal air cell drainage rather than the nasolacrimal duct.
notes.D: The sphenoethmoidal recess lies above the superior concha and receives drainage from the sphenoidal sinus.
notes.E: The hiatus semilunaris is a groove in the middle meatus involved in sinus drainage rather than tear drainage.

ana-g16-a156.why: As the external carotid artery courses forwards, the styloid apparatus and glossopharyngeal nerve separate it from the internal carotid. The vagus trunk remains inside the carotid sheath alongside the internal carotid.

notes.A: The styloid process projects downwards between the carotid arteries as part of the styloid apparatus.
