notes.B: Stylopharyngeus descends between the carotid arteries towards the lateral pharyngeal wall.
notes.C: Styloglossus passes forwards from the styloid process between the carotid arteries towards the tongue.
notes.D: The glossopharyngeal nerve descends between the carotid arteries on its way towards the pharynx and tongue.
notes.E: The vagus trunk remains within the carotid sheath; its pharyngeal branch may pass between the arteries.

ana-g16-c25.why: The inferior thyroid artery usually arises from the thyrocervical trunk of the first part of the subclavian artery. The superior thyroid artery, in contrast, usually arises from the external carotid.

notes.B: The superior thyroid artery typically arises near the beginning of the external carotid and supplies the thyroid's upper pole.
notes.C: The facial artery arises from the external carotid and supplies superficial structures of the face and submandibular region.
notes.D: The lingual artery is an anterior branch of the external carotid that supplies the tongue and floor of the mouth.
notes.E: The occipital artery arises posteriorly from the external carotid and supplies the posterior scalp and adjacent muscles.

ana-g16-c43.why: The facial artery winds around the inferior border of the mandible immediately anterior to masseter. Its superficial position against bone permits palpation or compression at this point.

notes.A: The superficial temporal artery can be palpated anterior to the ear as it crosses the zygomatic arch.
notes.B: The lingual artery runs deep towards the tongue, including a segment deep to hyoglossus, rather than crossing the mandible.
notes.C: The maxillary artery runs deep within the infratemporal and pterygopalatine fossae rather than across the mandibular border.
notes.D: The transverse facial artery runs across the cheek below the zygomatic arch, not around the lower mandibular border.

ana-g16-p39.why: The testicular artery descends retroperitoneally towards the deep inguinal ring and travels through the inguinal canal to the scrotum. Unlike the ovarian artery, it does not normally enter the true pelvic cavity.

notes.A: The internal iliac artery descends into the true pelvis and provides the principal arterial supply to pelvic structures.
notes.B: The median sacral artery descends in the midline over the anterior sacrum, entering the pelvic cavity.
notes.C: The superior rectal artery is the continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery and descends into the pelvis to supply the rectum.
notes.D: The ovarian artery passes across the pelvic brim and runs in the suspensory ligament of the ovary to its pelvic destination.

ana-g16-p60.why: The superior gluteal artery is usually a branch of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery. It exits through the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis with the superior gluteal nerve.

notes.B: The lesser sciatic foramen transmits the obturator internus tendon and returning pudendal neurovascular structures, not the superior gluteal artery.
notes.C: The obturator canal carries the obturator nerve and vessels from the pelvis into the medial thigh.
notes.D: The pudendal canal carries internal pudendal vessels and the pudendal nerve along the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa.
notes.E: The sacral foramina carry sacral nerve branches and associated vessels rather than the superior gluteal arterial trunk.

ana-g16-k84.why: The radial artery crosses the floor of the anatomical snuffbox over the scaphoid and trapezium. Much of the scaphoid receives blood entering distally, making the proximal fragment vulnerable after a waist fracture.

notes.A: The ulnar artery passes into the hand on the ulnar side of the wrist rather than crossing the snuffbox.
notes.B: The radial artery provides branches to the scaphoid, many of which enter its distal region and supply it retrogradely.
notes.C: Thenar branches supply the thumb-side palmar muscles; the main vessel crossing the snuffbox is the radial artery.

ana-g16-t23.why: The thoracic wall is supplied chiefly by anterior and posterior intercostal arteries. The internal thoracic and musculophrenic arteries supply anterior intercostal spaces, while the thoracic aorta supplies most posterior spaces.

notes.A: The internal thoracic artery gives anterior intercostal branches to the upper intercostal spaces.
notes.B: The inferior epigastric artery principally supplies the anterior abdominal wall, although it anastomoses with the superior epigastric artery.
notes.C: Posterior intercostal arteries supply the intercostal spaces, with most arising directly from the thoracic aorta.
notes.D: The thyrocervical trunk sends branches to the neck and scapula. The upper posterior intercostal supply comes via the costocervical trunk.
notes.E: The suprascapular artery chiefly supplies the scapular region rather than the intercostal muscles.

ana-ms15-27.why: Large elastic arteries accommodate pulsatile ventricular ejection through elastic lamellae, whereas muscular arteries regulate distribution through smooth muscle. All ordinary arterial lumina are lined by endothelium rather than mesothelium.

notes.A: Elastic lamellae in conducting arteries permit expansion during systole and recoil during diastole.
notes.B: Successive arterial branches generally become smaller in diameter as they approach the capillary beds.
notes.C: Smooth muscle predominates in muscular arteries, whereas elastic arteries contain abundant elastic lamellae.
notes.D: Endothelium lines blood vessels; mesothelium lines serous cavities such as the pleural cavity.
notes.E: Ordinary arteries lack serial valves because pressure gradients drive their flow; semilunar heart valves are at the ventricular outlets.

ana-ms15-28.why: The fibrous pericardium surrounds the heart in the middle mediastinum and anchors it to the central tendon and sternum. The parietal serous pericardium adheres to its inner surface.

notes.A: The anterior mediastinum lies between the sternum and anterior surface of the fibrous pericardium.
notes.B: The fibrous pericardium blends with the central tendon around the caval opening, anchoring the heart to the diaphragm.
notes.C: Sternopericardial ligaments attach the fibrous pericardium to the posterior surface of the sternum.
notes.D: The posterior mediastinum lies behind the pericardium and in front of the thoracic vertebral column.
notes.E: The parietal serous pericardium is firmly adherent to the fibrous pericardium, rather than loosely attached.

ana-ms15-29.why: Serous pericardial reflections around arterial and venous roots create the transverse and oblique sinuses. The visceral and parietal layers are continuous at these reflections, enclosing a potential fluid-filled cavity.

notes.A: The serous layers reflect into each other around arterial roots; the tunica intima lines the vessel lumen separately.
notes.B: The transverse sinus lies posterior to the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk and anterior to the superior vena cava.
notes.C: The oblique sinus forms between serous reflections around the pulmonary veins and inferior vena cava, rather than from the sinus venosus.
notes.D: The parietal and visceral serous layers remain continuous where they reflect around the venous roots.
notes.E: The oblique sinus is a blind recess posterior to the left atrium between the pulmonary venous reflections.

ana-ms15-30.why: Cardiac surfaces are named according to their anatomical relationships: sternocostal, diaphragmatic and pulmonary surfaces, with the posterior base largely formed by the left atrium. No standard medial surface is described.

notes.A: The posterior base is formed mainly by the left atrium and receives the pulmonary veins.
notes.B: The sternocostal surface faces the anterior thoracic wall and is formed largely by the right ventricle.
notes.C: The diaphragmatic surface rests on the diaphragm and consists chiefly of the left ventricle with part of the right ventricle.
notes.D: The left pulmonary surface faces the left lung and is formed mainly by the left ventricle.
notes.E: A distinct medial surface is not part of the standard anatomical description of the heart.

ana-ms15-31.why: The sternocostal surface faces the sternum and costal cartilages and is formed mainly by the right ventricle. It displays anterior coronary grooves and the auricles rather than posterior venous structures.

notes.A: The anterior interventricular groove separates the ventricular surfaces and contains the anterior interventricular vessels.
notes.B: The coronary sulcus separates atria from ventricles, with portions visible on the anterior surface.
notes.C: The right auricle projects anteriorly from the right atrium beside the ascending aorta.
notes.D: The inferior vena cava enters the right atrium from below. Its opening is inside the atrium.
notes.E: The coronary sinus runs in the posterior coronary sulcus and drains into the right atrium.

ana-ms15-33.why: The right atrium receives systemic and coronary venous blood and contains the fossa ovalis with its raised limbus. Pulmonary venous openings belong to the left atrium, while chordae and infundibulum belong to ventricles.

notes.A: The pulmonary veins normally open into the left atrium and carry oxygenated blood from the lungs.
notes.B: The coronary sinus opens into the right atrium near the inferior vena cava and tricuspid orifice.
notes.C: The infundibulum is the smooth right ventricular outflow tract leading to the pulmonary valve.
notes.D: The limbus is the raised margin around the fossa ovalis on the right atrial side of the interatrial septum.
notes.E: Chordae tendineae connect atrioventricular valve cusps to papillary muscles within the ventricles.

ana-ms15-75.why: The epidermis consists of avascular stratified squamous epithelium. Its living cells obtain oxygen and nutrients by diffusion from capillaries in the underlying dermis rather than from vessels within the epidermis.

notes.A: The conjunctival connective tissue contains capillary networks that supply its overlying epithelium.
notes.B: The suprarenal gland has extensive capillary and sinusoidal networks that support hormone secretion into blood.
notes.D: Hepatic sinusoids are specialised discontinuous capillary channels that exchange substances with hepatocytes.
notes.E: Cortical bone contains blood vessels within central and perforating canals that nourish the mineralised tissue.

ana-ms15-76.why: Most central nervous system capillaries have continuous endothelium with tight junctions and restricted transcytosis. This specialised endothelial barrier helps maintain the stable extracellular environment required by neurones.

notes.A: Continuous capillaries lack endothelial fenestrations; fenestrated capillaries have pores that facilitate exchange.
notes.C: Pulmonary alveolar capillaries have continuous endothelium forming part of the thin air–blood barrier.
notes.D: Skin capillaries are predominantly continuous, whereas fenestrated capillaries are typical of endocrine and absorptive organs.
notes.E: Sinusoids have wider channels and discontinuous endothelial or basal lamina features, unlike ordinary fenestrated capillaries.

ana-ms15-77.why: The deep palmar arterial arch lies deep to the long flexor tendons near the metacarpal bases. Its depth and overlying tissues prevent routine clinical palpation as a superficial pulse.

notes.A: The radial artery is palpable at the anterior wrist just lateral to the flexor carpi radialis tendon.
notes.B: The superficial temporal artery is palpable where it crosses the zygomatic arch anterior to the ear.
notes.C: The facial artery is palpable where it winds around the mandible immediately anterior to masseter.
notes.E: Dorsalis pedis is palpable on the dorsum of the foot, usually lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon.

ana-ms15-t16.why: The first part of the subclavian artery lies medial to anterior scalene and normally gives the vertebral artery, internal thoracic artery and thyrocervical trunk. The costocervical origin varies by side.

notes.A: The vertebral artery arises from the first part and ascends towards the cervical transverse foramina.
notes.B: The superior thoracic artery usually arises from the first part of the axillary artery, beyond the first rib.
notes.C: The internal thoracic artery arises from the first part and descends along the internal anterior thoracic wall.
notes.D: The thyrocervical trunk originates from the first part and supplies cervical and scapular structures through its branches.
notes.E: The thoracodorsal artery usually branches from the subscapular artery, which arises from the axillary artery.

ana-ms15-t26.why: The electrocardiogram records electrical activity: the P wave reflects atrial depolarisation, the QRS complex ventricular depolarisation and the T wave ventricular repolarisation. Intervals and segments help localise conduction abnormalities.

notes.A: A prolonged PR interval indicates delayed atrioventricular conduction, commonly at the atrioventricular node, rather than delayed sinoatrial firing.
notes.B: The T wave reflects the electrical recovery of the ventricular myocardium following depolarisation.
notes.C: The segment between the QRS complex and T wave represents the interval when most ventricular myocardium remains depolarised.
notes.D: QRS abnormalities generally reflect ventricular activation, conduction or myocardial changes rather than isolated left atrial disease.
notes.E: An absent or abnormal P wave usually reflects altered atrial activation or rhythm, not necessarily atrioventricular node dysfunction.

ana-ms15-t31.why: Valve sounds are heard best at characteristic chest-wall sites rather than directly over their anatomical positions. The aortic and pulmonary areas lie superiorly, while tricuspid and mitral areas lie more inferiorly.

notes.A: The aortic area is at the right second intercostal space immediately adjacent to the sternum.
notes.B: The pulmonary area is at the left second intercostal space immediately adjacent to the sternum.
notes.C: Tricuspid sounds are best heard near the lower left sternal border, typically the fourth or fifth intercostal space.
notes.D: Mitral sounds are best heard at the cardiac apex near the left fifth intercostal space and midclavicular line.
notes.E: The normal apex beat is usually felt in the left fifth intercostal space at or just medial to the midclavicular line.

ana-ms15-t36.why: An end artery supplies a territory without sufficient collateral arterial flow to sustain it after occlusion. Renal and splenic segmental arteries and the central retinal artery illustrate this vulnerability.

notes.A: Renal segmental arteries lack effective intersegmental arterial communications, so occlusion can cause a segmental infarct.
notes.B: Splenic segmental branches have limited effective collateral connections, making their territories susceptible to infarction.
notes.C: The penis receives communicating arterial branches, rather than being a classic example of end-arterial supply.
notes.D: The stomach has abundant arterial communications along both curvatures, providing collateral routes for blood flow.
notes.E: The central retinal artery supplies the inner retina with little effective collateral circulation.

ana-ms15-t91.why: Superficial veins and cutaneous arterial branches run within the thigh subcutaneous tissue. The saphenous opening, by contrast, is a defect in the underlying deep fascia lata.

notes.A: The great saphenous vein ascends superficially along the medial thigh before entering the femoral vein.
notes.B: The small saphenous vein usually ascends the posterior calf and terminates in the popliteal vein.
notes.C: The saphenous opening is a gap in fascia lata, which is deep to the subcutaneous tissue.
notes.D: The superficial epigastric artery ascends in superficial fascia towards the lower anterior abdominal wall.
notes.E: The superficial external pudendal artery crosses the superficial medial thigh towards the external genitalia.

ana-g16-a11.why: The deep palmar arch is formed predominantly by the radial artery and completed by the deep branch of the ulnar artery. The superficial arch is predominantly ulnar.

notes.A: The ulnar artery chiefly forms the superficial palmar arch; its deep branch contributes to the deep arch.

ana-g16-a15.why: At the inferior border of teres major, the basilic vein continues as the axillary vein, receiving the brachial veins. The axillary vein becomes subclavian at the lateral border of the first rib.

notes.B: The lower border of teres major is the conventional landmark for the beginning of the axillary vein.

ana-g16-a19.why: The femoral sheath contains the artery laterally, the vein centrally and the femoral canal medially. The canal allows expansion of the adjacent femoral vein and contains loose tissue and lymphatics.

notes.A: The canal lies medial to both femoral vessels, rather than between the artery and vein.

ana-g16-a33.why: Paraumbilical veins accompany the ligamentum teres within the falciform ligament and communicate with the left portal vein. Their connections to superficial abdominal veins provide a portosystemic collateral pathway.

notes.B: Paraumbilical veins accompany the round ligament to the left portal system and can carry flow towards superficial abdominal veins in portal hypertension.

ana-g16-a42.why: Near the sixth intercostal space, the internal thoracic artery divides into the musculophrenic and superior epigastric arteries. Anterior intercostal branches arise along the internal thoracic and musculophrenic routes.

notes.A: Anterior intercostal arteries are segmental branches. The internal thoracic artery ends by giving the superior epigastric and musculophrenic branches.

ana-g16-a45.why: The paired inferior phrenic arteries provide major arterial supply to the inferior surface of the diaphragm. Superior phrenic, intercostal and internal thoracic branches supplement the diaphragmatic circulation.

notes.A: Internal thoracic branches contribute through the musculophrenic and pericardiacophrenic arteries, but do not constitute the principal supply.

ana-g16-a52.why: The pulmonary valve projects behind the medial end of the left third costal cartilage near the sternum. Its sound is heard best in the left second intercostal space.

notes.A: The pulmonary valve has a left-sided surface projection, not one at the right third costal cartilage.

ana-g16-a53.why: During ventricular contraction, papillary muscles tense the chordae tendineae attached to atrioventricular valve cusps. This prevents the closed cusps from prolapsing into the atria under ventricular pressure.

notes.B: Papillary muscle contraction stabilises the valve cusps through the chordae tendineae rather than opening the valves.

ana-g16-a54.why: The atrioventricular bundle penetrates the fibrous cardiac skeleton and courses at the superior interventricular septum before dividing. The atrioventricular node, rather than the bundle, occupies the inferior atrial septal region.

notes.A: The bundle of His reaches the interventricular septum; the atrioventricular node is in the atrial septal region.

ana-g16-a56.why: The conus branch commonly arises early from the right coronary artery and supplies the right ventricular outflow tract. In some individuals it arises separately from the right aortic sinus.

notes.B: The conus artery typically branches near the origin of the right coronary artery to supply the infundibulum.

ana-g16-a72.why: The right ascending lumbar and right subcostal veins commonly unite to form the azygos vein. Their left-sided counterparts contribute to the hemiazygos vein, with variations in both origins.

notes.A: The right-sided union contributes to the azygos vein, whereas the hemiazygos vein originates on the left.

ana-g16-a79.why: In the usual arterial pattern, the basilar artery terminates by dividing into the posterior cerebral arteries. The internal carotid artery normally terminates as the anterior and middle cerebral arteries.

notes.A: The posterior cerebral artery normally arises from the basilar artery, although a fetal-type carotid supply is a recognised variant.

ana-g16-a91.why: Scrotal skin receives anterior scrotal branches from the external pudendal arteries and posterior scrotal branches from the internal pudendal artery. This differs from the arterial supply of the testes themselves.

notes.B: The femoral artery supplies anterior scrotal skin through external pudendal branches, and the internal pudendal supplies posterior skin.

ana-g16-a136.why: The aortic arch curves over the left lung root and pulmonary arterial bifurcation. The ligamentum arteriosum links the arch and pulmonary artery, while the phrenic and vagus nerves cross its lateral aspect.

notes.A: The pulmonary trunk divides beneath the aortic arch into right and left pulmonary arteries.
notes.B: The arch passes superior to the left lung root as it continues into the descending thoracic aorta.
notes.C: The ligamentum arteriosum joins the aortic isthmus to the left pulmonary artery immediately beneath the arch.
notes.D: The left vagus nerve crosses the lateral arch; its recurrent laryngeal branch loops beneath the arch.
notes.E: The left phrenic nerve crosses the lateral aspect of the arch anterior to the vagus nerve.

ana-g16-k86.why: Axillary nodes are organised into pectoral, subscapular, humeral, central and apical groups. Most lymph from the upper limb and breast passes through these groups before reaching the subclavian lymphatic trunk.

notes.A: Central nodes receive lymph from the pectoral, humeral and subscapular axillary groups.
notes.B: Humeral nodes lie near the axillary vein and drain most lymph from the upper limb.
notes.C: Supraclavicular nodes are located in the lower neck, beyond the axillary nodal groups.

ana-g16-t24.why: Superficial chest-wall lymph drains mainly to axillary nodes, while deeper intercostal tissues drain towards parasternal and intercostal nodes. Breast lymph may also reach supraclavicular nodes via higher nodal pathways.

notes.A: Most superficial thoracic lymph reaches axillary rather than parasternal nodes.
notes.B: Pectoral axillary nodes receive lymph from the superficial anterior thoracic wall and the supraumbilical region of the anterior abdominal wall.
notes.C: Deep intercostal tissues drain chiefly to intercostal and parasternal nodes rather than superficial axillary pathways.
notes.D: Breast lymph can reach supraclavicular nodes through apical axillary and other communicating lymphatic pathways.
notes.E: Superficial lymph from the upper back generally reaches subscapular axillary nodes rather than superficial inguinal nodes.

ana-ms15-98.why: Lymph converges through regional trunks into two principal collecting ducts, with considerable anatomical variation in their termination. Hundreds of lymph nodes filter lymph along these regional drainage pathways.

notes.A: The conventional named trunks include paired jugular, subclavian, bronchomediastinal and lumbar trunks, as well as the intestinal trunk.
notes.B: The thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct represent the two conventional main collecting pathways.
notes.C: The human body contains several hundred lymph nodes, commonly estimated at approximately six hundred.

ana-ms15-100.why: Primary lymphoid organs provide environments for lymphocyte development and antigen-independent maturation. B lymphocytes mature in the bone marrow, while T-cell precursors migrate to the thymus for maturation and selection.

notes.A: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs where mature lymphocytes encounter antigens carried in lymph.
notes.B: Red bone marrow produces lymphocyte precursors and provides the site of B-cell development and maturation.
notes.C: The thymus provides the specialised environment for T-cell maturation and selection.

ana-ms15-t66.why: Regional lymphatic drainage follows characteristic nodal pathways before entering the major lymphatic trunks. Most breast lymph drains to pectoral axillary nodes, while head and neck lymph passes through cervical nodes.

notes.A: The right jugular trunk can join the right lymphatic duct or empty independently at the right venous angle.
notes.B: Humeral axillary nodes are deep within the axilla and receive lymph from superficial and deep upper-limb vessels.
notes.C: Subpyloric nodes drain towards hepatic and coeliac nodal pathways rather than directly to the lumbar nodes.
notes.D: The jugulodigastric node belongs to the upper deep cervical chain and receives lymph from pharyngeal structures.
notes.E: Most breast lymph reaches the pectoral axillary group, not the humeral group that principally drains the arm.

ana-gpq-26.why: Waldeyer’s ring is a collection of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue around the entrance to the respiratory and digestive tracts. It includes pharyngeal, tubal, palatine and lingual tonsillar tissue.

notes.A: The palatine tonsils lie in the lateral oropharynx between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches.
notes.B: The lingual tonsil comprises lymphoid nodules at the posterior part of the tongue.
notes.C: The jugulodigastric node is a deep cervical lymph node that receives tonsillar drainage, not tonsillar tissue.
notes.D: Submental nodes drain structures such as the chin and lower lip rather than forming the pharyngeal lymphoid ring.
notes.E: Tubal tonsillar tissue surrounds the pharyngeal opening of the auditory tube in the nasopharynx.

ana-gpq-76.why: Superficial inguinal nodes comprise a horizontal group below the inguinal ligament and a vertical group beside the great saphenous vein. They drain superficial lower-limb, lower abdominal and perineal territories.

notes.A: The horizontal group lies parallel to and just inferior to the inguinal ligament.
notes.B: The vertical group lies along the terminal great saphenous vein in the proximal thigh.
notes.C: External genital skin generally drains to medial horizontal nodes, while lateral nodes receive gluteal and lateral abdominal drainage.
notes.D: The medial horizontal group receives superficial lymph from the lower anterior abdomen. Lateral abdominal territories may drain to the lateral horizontal nodes.
notes.E: Most superficial lower-limb lymph reaches the vertical group, except some vessels accompanying the small saphenous vein.

ana-gpq-159.why: The spleen lies in the left hypochondrium with its long axis approximately parallel to the tenth rib. Its visceral surface bears impressions from the stomach, left kidney and colonic flexure.

notes.A: The long splenic axis runs approximately along the tenth rib, between the ninth and eleventh ribs.
notes.B: The phrenicocolic ligament forms a supporting shelf beneath the inferior aspect of the spleen.
notes.C: The colic impression on the visceral surface is related to the left colic flexure.
notes.D: The gastric impression occupies the broad concavity between the hilum and superior border.
notes.E: The renal impression lies posterior to the hilum and contacts the upper left kidney.

ana-osa-51.why: Superficial lymph from the upper posterior trunk generally drains to the subscapular axillary nodes. These lie along the posterior axillary fold and pass lymph to central and apical nodes.

notes.A: Superficial inguinal nodes receive lymph chiefly from the lower trunk, perineum and superficial lower limb.
notes.B: Pectoral axillary nodes primarily receive lymph from the anterior thoracic wall and breast.
notes.C: External iliac nodes receive deep inguinal and pelvic drainage. Upper-back skin generally drains through the axilla.
notes.E: Deep cervical nodes principally drain head and neck structures rather than the upper posterior thoracic wall.

ana-g16-a34.why: Superficial lymphatic collectors generally accompany superficial veins in the subcutaneous tissues. Deep lymphatic vessels more often accompany major arteries and veins supplying or draining deeper structures.

notes.A: Superficial lymphatics are associated with superficial veins, while deep lymphatics accompany deeper neurovascular bundles.

ana-g16-a60.why: When a cisterna chyli is present, its upper end continues as the thoracic duct near the thoracolumbar junction. The duct enters the thorax through the aortic hiatus at approximately T12, while the reservoir's level varies.

notes.B: The cisterna chyli continues into the thoracic duct near the aortic hiatus when this lymphatic reservoir is present.

ana-ms15-55.why: The thyroid gland lies immediately anterior and lateral to the upper trachea. Enlargement, especially with retrosternal extension, can narrow or displace the tracheal lumen and compromise airflow.

notes.B: A thoracic aortic aneurysm can compress the intrathoracic trachea. Thyroid enlargement is a common cause of compression in the lower neck.
notes.C: Aortic coarctation is a narrowing of the aortic lumen rather than a typical compressive mass.
notes.D: A retropharyngeal abscess can obstruct the upper airway by bulging into the pharynx rather than primarily compressing the trachea.
notes.E: Horner syndrome reflects interrupted sympathetic innervation and is not itself a mass that compresses the airway.

ana-ms15-57.why: The inferior thoracic aperture is bounded posteriorly by T12 and anteriorly by the xiphisternal region. Its posterior boundary lies lower than its anterior boundary, with the diaphragm closing the opening.

notes.A: The inferior aperture slopes downwards posteriorly because its vertebral boundary lies below the anterior boundary.
notes.C: The posterior boundary is formed by the twelfth thoracic vertebra rather than two vertebral bodies.
notes.D: The lateral boundaries are formed by the costal margins as well as the eleventh and twelfth ribs.
notes.E: The anterior boundary is the xiphisternal region, with the costal margins forming anterolateral boundaries.
